entry: Landlocked state in eastern [[Germany]]. Its capital is [[Dresden]], and its largest city is [[Leipzig]]. With an area of 18,450 square kilometres (7,124 sq mi) and more than 4 million inhabitants, it is Germany's tenth largest state by area. The name derives from the historic Electorate and Kingdom of Saxony, ruled by the House of Wettin. After the [[Congress of Vienna]] in 1815 the kingdom ceded much of its territory to [[Prussia]]. Following World War II the region became part of [[East Germany]] until the state was abolished in 1952; it was re-established upon [[German reunification]] in 1990.

Landlocked state of [[Germany]]. Its capital is Magdeburg. It covers an area of 20,555 square kilometres (7,936 sq mi) and has about 2.14 million inhabitants. The state was formed in July 1945 by the Soviet army administration from the former Prussian Province of [[Saxony]] and the Free State of Anhalt. It was dissolved in 1952 and re-established in 1990 upon [[German reunification]]. Six [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage sites]] lie within it, including the Bauhaus sites in Dessau and the Dessau-Wörlitz Garden Realm. The Harz mountains rise in the southwest; their highest peak, the Brocken, reaches 1,141 meters (3,735 ft).

Single-reed [[Woodwind instrument|woodwind]] instrument with a conical body, usually made of [[Brass|brass]]. Sound is produced when a reed on the mouthpiece vibrates inside the body, and pitch is controlled by opening and closing holes along the tube with leather pads operated by keys. Belgian instrument maker Adolphe Sax invented it in the early 1840s and patented it on 28 June 1846. The modern family consists entirely of B♭ and E♭ instruments; the B♭ soprano, E♭ alto, B♭ tenor and E♭ baritone are the most widely used. It is used in [[Classical music|classical music]], military and marching bands, [[Jazz|jazz]] and contemporary music, and as a solo or horn-section voice in some [[Rock and roll|rock and roll]] and popular music.

Egyptian political theorist and revolutionary, and a leading member of the [[Muslim Brotherhood]]. He wrote 24 published books and at least 581 articles, and is best known for his work on the social and political role of [[Islam]], notably *Social Justice* and *Milestones*. His magnum opus, *In the Shade of the Qur'an*, is a 30-volume commentary on the [[Quran]]. He saw the society of the [[United States]] as materialistic and advocated offensive *jihad*. In 1966 he was convicted of plotting to assassinate President [[Gamal Abdel Nasser]] and was executed by [[Hanging|hanging]]. Followers regard him as a martyr, while Western observers see him as a key originator of Islamist ideology and an inspiration for militant groups such as [[Al-Qaeda]]. His ideas on *jahiliyya* and the linking of [[Sharia]] with *tawhid* have strongly influenced Islamist and jihadist movements.

Contagious human skin infestation caused by the [[Mite|mite]] *Sarcoptes scabiei* var. *hominis*, measuring 0.2–0.45 mm. The most common symptoms are severe itching, often worse at night, and a pimple-like rash. Symptoms usually appear within three weeks of a first infection and within 24 hours of a second. They result from an allergic reaction to the mites, of which often only 10–15 are involved. Scabies spreads through prolonged direct skin contact (at least 10 minutes) and is a particular [[Public health|public health]] problem in crowded settings such as care homes, schools, prisons and hospitals. It occurs more commonly in the developing world and in [[Tropical climate|tropical climates]]. Treatment includes oral and topical [[Ivermectin|ivermectin]] and permethrin. As of 2015 about 204 million people, or 2.8% of the world population, were affected.

Temporary structure used to support workers and materials during the construction, maintenance and repair of [[Building|buildings]], bridges and other structures. Unsafe scaffolding can cause death or serious injury. Adapted forms are used for formwork, shoring, grandstand seating and concert stages. Early scaffolding was made of [[Wood|wood]] secured with [[Rope|rope]] knots. Sockets in the walls around [[Paleolithic]] cave paintings at Lascaux suggest a scaffold was used over 17,000 years ago. The Berlin Foundry Cup depicts scaffolding in [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]] in the early 5th century BC. David Henry Jones and Daniel Palmer Jones patented the Scaffixer coupling in either 1907 or 1910. The Universal Coupler of 1919, by Palmer-Jones, became the industry standard.

Small insect of the order [[Hemiptera]], comprising about 8,000 described species. Adult females typically have soft, limbless bodies concealed under domed wax scales, while males have legs, sometimes wings, and resemble small flies. Scale insects feed on plant sap, and the excess fluid they excrete as honeydew encourages sooty mold. They often have a mutualistic relationship with [[Ant|ants]], which feed on the honeydew and protect the insects from predators. The oldest fossils, preserved in [[Amber]], date to the Late Jurassic. The cottony cushion scale is a serious pest of [[Citrus]] fruit trees, while other species are used for biological control of the [[Opuntia|prickly pear]]. Some species yield [[Dye|dyes]] such as carmine and kermes, and [[Shellac]] lacquer. The red colour-names crimson and scarlet both derive from the names of kermes products in other languages.

Physical model geometrically similar to its prototype. Models built to the same scale as the prototype are called mockups. Scale is expressed as a ratio such as 1:8, or in English-speaking countries as feet per inch, so that 1:48 means 1 inch to 4 feet. Scale models are used in [[Engineering|engineering]] design and testing, sales, filmmaking special effects, military strategy and hobbies such as [[Rail transport|rail transport]] modeling. Hobbyists build them from kits, by scratch building or by collecting pre-assembled models. The Boy Scouts of America's annual Pinewood Derby, which debuted in 1953, has Cub Scouts race gravity-powered cars carved from [[Pine|pine]] wood. Regulations generally limit a car's weight to 5 ounces (141.7 g).

Consecutive series of musical notes that form a progression between one note and its octave. The word derives from the Latin *scala*, meaning ladder. Scales are distinguished by their step pattern, the intervals between successive notes. A chromatic scale has a semitone step throughout, while the major scale follows the pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. In the [[Classical music|classical]] common-practice period, most or all of a work's [[Melody|melody]] and [[Harmony|harmony]] was often built from a single scale. A specific scale is defined by its interval pattern and its tonic, or first degree, so C major is a major scale beginning on C. Scales may also be classified by the number of pitch classes per octave, from the seven-note heptatonic scale, the most common modern Western scale, to the five-note pentatonic scale.

Small rigid plate made of keratin that grows out of the [[Skin|skin]] of [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]] to provide protection. Scales have evolved multiple times through convergent evolution, with varying structure and function. In [[Lepidoptera|butterflies and moths]], scales are made of [[Chitin|chitin]] and cover the wings, providing coloration. Fish scales are dermally derived. Placoid scales, found on [[Shark|sharks]] and [[Stingray|stingrays]], are similar in structure to teeth. Leptoid scales of higher bony fish are cycloid, with smooth edges as in salmon and carp, or ctenoid, with toothed edges. Reptile scales are epidermal, and in crocodilians and turtles they overlie osteoderms, in which case they are more properly termed scutes.

Marine bivalve [[Mollusca|mollusc]] of the family Pectinidae, found in all the world's oceans but never in fresh water. The majority of species live recumbent on sandy substrates, though many are free-living and can swim short distances. When a predator such as a [[Starfish|starfish]] approaches, a scallop may escape by jet propulsion, clapping its shells together. Unlike most other bivalves, all scallops have a ring of numerous simple [[Eye|eyes]] around the edge of the mantle. Many species are prized as food, and the adductor muscle, sold as [[Seafood|seafood]], is also called a scallop. Some species are farmed. Their fan-shaped shells have been used as motifs in art, architecture and design since ancient times.

Subregion of northern Europe, most commonly comprising Denmark, Norway and Sweden, which share strong historical, cultural and linguistic ties. The term may also refer to the Scandinavian Peninsula. In English usage it is sometimes a synonym for the [[Nordic countries]], and Iceland and the Faroe Islands are sometimes included. Some authors also count Finland as Scandinavian because of its economic and cultural similarities. Most people live in the temperate south, while the north has long, cold winters. During the [[Viking Age]], Scandinavian peoples raided, colonized and traded across Europe, and they were the first Europeans to reach North America. The Kalmar Union of Denmark, Norway and Sweden lasted for over 100 years until Sweden left it under Gustav I. The union between Sweden and Norway ended in 1905. Today the countries have some of Europe's strongest economies and generous welfare systems, sometimes called the *Nordic model*.

Mountain range running through the Scandinavian Peninsula, also known as the Scandes. Its western sides drop steeply into the North Sea and Norwegian Sea, forming the [[Fjord|fjords]] of Norway, while to the northeast it curves toward [[Finland]]. To the north it forms the border between [[Norway]] and [[Sweden]], reaching 2,000 metres (6,600 ft) at the [[Arctic Circle]]. Although relatively high for a range so young, it is very steep in places. Galdhøpiggen in southern Norway, at 2,469 metres (8,100 ft), is the highest peak in mainland Northern Europe. Kebnekaise is the highest peak on the Swedish side, at 2,096.8 metres (6,879 ft), and Halti, at 1,324 metres (4,344 ft), is the highest point in Finland, although its peak lies in Norway.

Literature written in the languages of the [[Nordic countries]] of northern Europe, which are mostly North Germanic, along with Finnish, Sami and Greenlandic. The earliest written records are runic inscriptions, and Eddic poems, believed to date from the 9th century, survive in 13th-century manuscripts. The 13th century was a golden age of Icelandic literature, with [[Snorri Sturluson]]'s *Prose Edda* and *Heimskringla*. [[Henrik Ibsen]], a Norwegian playwright, was largely responsible for the popularity of modern realistic drama in Europe, with plays such as *The Wild Duck* and *A Doll's House*. Danish writers include [[Hans Christian Andersen]] and [[Søren Kierkegaard]]. [[Nobel Prize|Nobel Prizes]] in Literature have gone to many Scandinavian writers, including Selma Lagerlöf, Knut Hamsun and Halldór Laxness.

Silvery-white [[Metal|metallic]] chemical element with symbol Sc and atomic number 21, found in the d-block of the [[Periodic table]]. It is usually classified as a [[Rare-earth element|rare-earth element]], together with [[Yttrium|yttrium]] and the lanthanides. Scandium was discovered in 1879 by spectral analysis of the minerals euxenite and gadolinite from [[Scandinavia]]. It is present in most deposits of rare-earth and uranium compounds, but is extracted from them in only a few mines. Metallic scandium was first prepared in 1937, and applications were not developed until the 1970s, when its positive effects on [[Aluminium|aluminium]] alloys were discovered; these alloys remain its only major use. Global trade in scandium oxide totals 15–20 tonnes per year. Its properties are intermediate between those of aluminium and yttrium.

Long piece of fabric worn on or around the neck, shoulders or head, used for warmth, sun protection, cleanliness, fashion, religious reasons or to show support for a sports team. Scarves are made from wool, linen, silk or cotton. In [[Ancient Egypt]], [[Nefertiti]] is said to have worn a tightly woven headscarf in 1350 BC. In [[Ancient Rome]], a scarf was used to wipe sweat from the neck and face. Croatian soldiers, some of them mercenaries in France, wore scarves called cravats, the precursor to the necktie. [[Napoleon]] bought Egyptian scarves for his wife, Empress Josephine, who is believed to have acquired over 400 of them. The scarf became a fashion accessory by the early 19th century. During [[World War I]] and [[World War II]], women in the United States knitted scarves for soldiers.

Infectious disease caused by *Streptococcus pyogenes*, a Group A streptococcus. It most commonly affects children between 5 and 15 years of age and typically develops in people who have strep throat or streptococcal skin infections. Symptoms include sore throat, fever, headache, swollen lymph nodes and a characteristic red rash that feels like sandpaper. The rash results from damage to [[Capillary|capillaries]] by exotoxins. The bacteria are usually spread by coughing or sneezing. There is no [[Vaccine|vaccine]]; prevention relies on handwashing and avoiding others when sick, while [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]] treat the disease and prevent most complications. Long-term complications include kidney disease, rheumatic fever and [[Arthritis|arthritis]]. Scarlet fever was a leading cause of death in children in the early 20th century, but its severity was already declining before [[World War II]] and the introduction of antibiotics. Occurrence in the U.K. rose by 68% between 2014 and 2018.

American actress, singer, producer and director. Her films as a leading actress have grossed over $15.4 billion worldwide. She portrayed Natasha Romanoff, also known as Black Widow, in eight films of the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]]. She won a British Academy Film Award for *Lost in Translation* and a Tony Award for the Broadway revival of *A View from the Bridge*. She received two simultaneous [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nominations, for *Marriage Story* and *Jojo Rabbit*. She was the world's highest-paid actress in 2018, 2019 and 2025.

Range of physical processes in which moving particles or radiation are deflected from a straight trajectory, or blocked, by localized non-uniformities in the medium they pass through. Originally confined to light, the term reaches back at least to [[Isaac Newton]] in the 17th century. [[William Herschel]] applied it to heat rays in 1800. Near the end of the 19th century the scattering of cathode rays and [[X-ray|X-rays]] was observed, and with the discovery of subatomic particles, such as by [[Ernest Rutherford]] in 1911, the term broadened. Scattering theory is significant in [[Radar|radar]] sensing and [[Medical ultrasound|medical ultrasound]]. In particle physics, the S-matrix, introduced by John Archibald Wheeler and [[Werner Heisenberg]], describes the quantum interaction of fundamental particles.

Animal that feeds on dead and decaying organic matter, including carrion, rotting plants and refuse. Carrion-eating scavengers are called necrophages. Obligate carrion scavengers, such as Old and New World [[Vulture|vultures]], rely on carcasses, while most vertebrate carrion eaters are facultative scavengers that also hunt. [[Hyena|Hyenas]] and [[Jackal|jackals]] are examples, and large predators such as [[Lion|lions]], [[Leopard|leopards]] and [[Wolf|wolves]] will scavenge if given the chance, sometimes intimidating the original hunters into abandoning their kills. Burying beetles are obligate necrophages. By removing decaying matter, scavengers help recycle nutrients and keep it from accumulating in ecosystems.

Group of 29 European countries that have abolished border controls at their common borders. The area takes its name from the 1985 Schengen Agreement and the 1990 Schengen Convention, both signed in Schengen, Luxembourg. It functions mostly as a single jurisdiction under a common visa policy for international travel. All but two of the 27 [[European Union|EU]] member states belong to it; Cyprus and Ireland do not. Non-EU members [[Iceland]], [[Liechtenstein]], [[Norway]] and [[Switzerland]] have also signed association agreements. The area has a population of more than 450 million people.

1993 American historical drama film directed by [[Steven Spielberg]], based on Thomas Keneally's novel *Schindler's Ark*. It follows [[Oskar Schindler]], a German industrialist who saved more than a thousand mostly Polish-Jewish refugees from the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]] by employing them in his factories during [[World War II]]. Shot in black and white, it stars [[Liam Neeson]] and [[Ben Kingsley]]. It won seven [[Academy Awards]], including Best Picture, and earned $322.2 million worldwide on a $22 million budget. The Library of Congress selected it for preservation in 2004.

Division between people, usually within an organization, movement or religious denomination. The word is most often applied to a split in a single religious body, such as the [[East–West Schism]] in [[Christianity]] or the Sunni–Shia divide in [[Islam]]. It is also used of splits in non-religious organizations and of separations between friends or lovers. In [[Buddhism]], schism is a strict legal term defined by differences in the interpretation of monastic rules within one community rather than by doctrine; the Theravada canon defines it as nine or more monks separating and performing their own services. In Roman Catholicism, every [[Heresy|heresy]] is a schism, though not every schism is a heresy. Schisms frequently involve mutual accusations of heresy, and a schismatic is often a pejorative label.

Medium-grained [[Metamorphic rock|metamorphic rock]] with pronounced schistosity, meaning it splits easily into thin flakes or plates. Schist is generally derived from fine-grained sedimentary rock such as [[Shale|shale]], and it can also form from igneous [[Tuff|tuffs]]. Its texture reflects a high content of platy minerals such as [[Mica|mica]], talc, chlorite or graphite, often interleaved with granular minerals such as [[Feldspar|feldspar]] or [[Quartz|quartz]]. It typically forms during regional metamorphism accompanying mountain building. Schist bedrock can pose a challenge for [[Civil engineering|civil engineering]] because of its pronounced planes of weakness.

Condition marked by extreme asociality, emotional coldness and detachment, alongside a rich internal fantasy world. Symptoms typically begin in late childhood or adolescence, and the cause is uncertain, though a neglectful childhood, genetics and neurological factors are implicated. Shared genetic risks link it to [[Schizophrenia|schizophrenia]]. It is diagnosed by clinical observation and can be hard to distinguish from [[Autism|autism]]. Because people rarely seek treatment, the effectiveness of therapy and medication has not been well studied. Studies generally report a prevalence of less than 1%.
